turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

Yeah, "handle" is never a small ask — it means your director wants results, not a relationship-preserving conversation. And with Suresh-ji, you're not just managing a slipping module, you're managing 19 years of history that you didn't create and can't casually override.

Can I ask something first — do you actually know *why* his module is slipping? Like specifically. Is it a skills gap, is he stretched across too much legacy stuff, is he checked out, is there something personal going on, or is the scope of what he owns just unrealistic for one person at this point? Because "handle" can mean very different conversations depending on the answer — coaching, redistributing work, performance managing, or even just you advocating upward that the timeline was wrong to begin with.

What's your read on it, honestly?

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

That's a real bind — not just professionally awkward but genuinely painful. He showed up for you when you were vulnerable and new, and now you're the one holding the numbers that could hurt him. It makes sense you're dreading this.

But I want to gently push on something: the debt you feel to him is real, and it doesn't mean you owe him silence. If anything, it means you owe him honesty and respect — the same thing he'd want for himself if he were managing someone he cared about. Covering for him, softening it into vagueness, or letting your director "handle" it over your head would actually be worse for him than a direct, humane conversation with you.

The slide of defect metrics doesn't have to be the opening move. What if the conversation started with what's true — that you respect him, that this is hard for you to raise precisely *because* of your history, and that you need to understand what's going on with him before jumping to metrics at all? Ask him directly: is he overloaded, stuck on something technically, distracted by something outside work, disengaged? He's been doing this 19 years — he probably already knows the releases have slipped. He may even be relieved someone asks him directly instead of talking around him.

Have you thought about how you'd open it — with the data, or with the relationship?

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

I'm not going to just say yes, because I think you're using "the books say so" to skip the actual hard part, which is figuring out what's happening with Suresh-ji, not just how to deliver the message.

The books aren't wrong about directness. But directness without understanding isn't candor, it's just efficient. Walking in cold with a slide of defect metrics to a 56-year-old man who's been there 19 years, calls you like a daughter, and has never had a manager younger than him before — that's going to land as a performance, not a conversation. Even if every word is "professional and kind," he'll feel the distance, and he'll feel it especially because it's you.

So here's what I'd actually say: yes, be direct — eventually. But Monday's meeting should probably start with a question, not a slide. Something like: "Suresh-ji, I've been looking at the last two releases, and I need to understand what's going on with your module — not to point fingers, but because I need your help fixing it." Let him talk first. Then bring the specifics once you know what you're actually dealing with.

You can still leave that room having stated expectations clearly. You just don't have to open with the scorecard to prove you're being candid. Does that distinction land, or does it still feel like I'm dodging your question?

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

There isn't one. I want to say that plainly, because I think you're searching for a version of this where you come out clean, and it doesn't exist. Either you hold him accountable and risk being the person who ended his run, or you protect him and fail your team and your own integrity as a manager. Both have a cost. You don't get to pick the option with no cost, only the one whose cost you can live with.

Here's the thing though — being "the villain" in his eyes, or your own head at 2am, isn't the same as actually being one. If you do this with real effort — you understood him, you gave him a genuine chance, you didn't hide behind process, you were honest instead of quietly maneuvering him out — and it still ends in a PIP, that's not you using good manners to knife him. That's you doing your job while refusing to pretend the relationship doesn't exist. Those aren't contradictory.

The "move the module and let him coast" option feels kind, but sit with what it actually is: you deciding, without telling him, that he's past being useful, and quietly managing him into irrelevance instead of talking to him like the adult and colleague he is. That's arguably more disrespectful than a hard conversation, because it takes away his agency to even try.

You keep asking how to not be the villain. I don't think that's answerable. The better question is: what would make you someone Suresh-ji himself would say treated him fairly, even if the outcome is bad? What would that need to look like on your end?
